source: National Curriculum (Art and Design). lessons.unit: Unit 1: Islamic geometric design
lessons.title: The eight-pointed star: construction
objectives: Describe how geometry is used in Islamic art
Construct an eight-pointed star with ruler, protractor and compass
Check accuracy and refine lines

keywords.def: the mathematics of shapes, lines and angles
a light line used to build a design and later erased

starter: Bismillah. What is the radius of a circle?
How many degrees in a right angle?

teach.heading: Geometry in Islamic art
bullets: Artists used circles, squares and stars
teach.note: Show tiles and woodwork on screen. Say the tradition often avoids images of living things and focuses on geometry and calligraphy. Pupils need paper, pencil, ruler, compass, protractor, black pen, colours.

teach.heading: Step 1: circle and axes
bullets: Draw a circle with radius 6 cm
teach.note: Model slowly. Use very light pencil because these are construction lines.

teach.heading: Step 2: eight points
bullets: Use a protractor from the centre
This gives eight points on the circle
teach.note: Check: 360 divided by 8 is 45. Misconception: measuring from the edge instead of the centre.

teach.heading: Step 3: two squares
bullets: Join the other four for a second square
teach.note: Show how the two squares overlap to form the star. Name it: eight-pointed star (octagram), often called khatam in design traditions.

teach.heading: Refine and outline
bullets: Go over the star in black pen
Check every line meets a point
teach.note: Self-assess accuracy. Success criteria: points exact, lines straight, clean outline.

practice: How many degrees between eight equally spaced points on a circle?
independent: Draw a circle and mark eight points with a protractor.
Join the points to form two squares.
exit: Complete your eight-pointed star neatly in black pen.
Write two sentences explaining why geometry matters in Islamic design.
homework: How do you find the angle between eight points?
Which points do you join to make a square?
lessons.send: Practise the construction again at home with a different circle size.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Islamic geometric design
lessons.title: Developing the star: layers, colour and repeat
objectives: Add inner lines to develop the star
Apply colour with a clear plan
Explore how repeats fit together

keywords.def: to build on a design to make it richer
a clear difference, such as light against dark
to use a design again to cover a surface

starter: Describe the steps to construct the star.
How many sides has an octagon?
What is a complementary colour pair?

teach.heading: Look at your star
bullets: Lines cross to make smaller shapes
teach.note: Pupils have their star from last lesson. Ask them to count the shapes inside.

teach.heading: Adding inner lines
bullets: Draw parallel lines inside each point
Make a band that weaves over and under
Erase gaps for the over-under effect
teach.note: Model one weave. Misconception: all lines should be solid; gaps show weaving.

teach.heading: Colour plan
bullets: Keep matching shapes the same colour
teach.note: Show a plan on small thumbnail first. Link to Y6 colour wheel.

teach.heading: Repeating the star
bullets: Draw four stars touching at the tips
Look at the shapes between them
Fill the gaps with a new motif
teach.note: This shows how a design extends into a repeat. Pupils sketch only, do not need to finish.

teach.heading: Evaluate
teach.note: Use a peer or teacher comment structure: what went well, even better if.

practice: Name the shape inside an eight-pointed star.
independent: Draw inner parallel lines on one point of your star.
Plan your colours in a thumbnail sketch.
exit: Colour your star using your plan and finish the weave effect.
Sketch four stars touching and design a filler shape.
homework: Why use contrast in a design?
What target will you set for your next design?
lessons.send: Find a pattern in a building or object at home and sketch its repeat.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Abstract art, still life and analogous colour
lessons.title: What is abstract art? Feeling through line, shape and colour
lessons.bigQuestion: Can a single wavy blue line make you feel calm? Can a jagged red one make you feel anxious? Why?
objectives: To understand how abstract artists express a feeling using line, shape and colour instead of recognisable things
successCriteria: All: describe the difference between realistic and abstract art
Most: choose lines, shapes and colours to show a given feeling
Some: explain how another artist's abstract choices create a mood
lessons.crossCurricular: English: choosing precise words to describe mood and atmosphere
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the abstract tradition of Islamic geometric and arabesque art

keywords.def: art that does not show recognisable things, using line, shape and colour
the feeling a piece of art gives
made of regular shapes like circles, squares and triangles

hook.text: Can a single wavy blue line make you feel calm? Can a jagged red one make you feel anxious? Why?
hook.a: Line direction and colour carry feelings: soft curves and cool colours calm; sharp angles and hot colours excite.

islamicLink.text: Islamic art has a long abstract tradition: geometric patterns, arabesque (plant-based) designs and calligraphy fill masjids from Cordoba to Isfahan. Rather than picturing living beings, artists used pattern and rhythm to point to order, unity and the infinite, a fitting starting point for abstract art.

starter.a: Colours next to each other on the colour wheel.
options: Colours next to each other on the wheel

starter.q: Name the vanishing point's line in perspective.
Name one Islamic art form we studied.
starter.a: Geometric pattern, arabesque, mosaic, tessellation or calligraphy.
Shapes that fit together with no gaps or overlaps.

teach.heading: Realistic or abstract?
bullets: Realistic: looks like the real thing
Abstract: line, shape and colour for their own sake
teach.note: Show a photo of a still life and an abstract geometric design side by side.

right.title: Abstract
points: Shapes and colours chosen for feeling

teach.heading: Line and shape carry feeling
bullets: Zig-zags and sharp angles: energy, tension
teach.note: Wassily Kandinsky wrote about colour and shape expressing feeling; show one of his geometric compositions (no figures).

teach.heading: Colour carries feeling
bullets: Dark tones: serious; light tones: hopeful
teach.note: Feelings vary between people: we justify, not just claim.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which choice best shows 'calm'?
check.why: Horizontal curves and cool colours read as calm; the others show energy or tension.

practice.q: Draw four small boxes: calm, angry, joyful, anxious. Use only line (pencil) in each.
practice.a: Calm: horizontals; angry: jagged; joyful: rising curves; anxious: tight scribbles.
practice.model: Teacher draws 'calm' with long horizontal waves and 'angry' with heavy zig-zags, saying why.

practice.q: Add colour to two of your boxes and explain one choice.
practice.a: For example: blue for calm because cool colours feel peaceful.

independent.q: Core: Make an A5 abstract piece that expresses one feeling, using at least three kinds of line and shape and a chosen colour palette.
independent.a: An abstract piece with deliberate line, shape and colour for one feeling.
independent.model: Teacher plans 'gratitude' aloud: rising curves, warm gold and soft green, a circle for wholeness.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, explain your choices. Start: 'I chose... lines because...'
independent.a: For example: I chose rising curved lines because they feel uplifting.

exit.q: Abstract art... A) always shows people B) uses line, shape and colour instead of recognisable things C) is only black and white
exit.a: B) uses line, shape and colour instead of recognisable things
options: Uses line, shape and colour instead of recognisable things

exit.q: Big question: can a single line make you feel calm? Explain with one example.
exit.a: Yes: a soft horizontal blue wave feels calm because it is gentle and cool.

lessons.homework: Make a 'feelings line' strip: eight short lines, each labelled with the feeling it shows.
lessons.send: SEND: feeling words with example lines. EAL: calm, angry, joyful, anxious with images. Stretch: compare Kandinsky with a geometric Islamic panel.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 8 (abstract art; analogous hues)
At home: sketchbook or A4 paper, pencils, coloured pencils or paints, ruler, three household objects
Line and feeling worksheet (pupil PDF)

pictures.alt: A geometric pattern on a masjid ceiling

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Abstract art, still life and analogous colour
lessons.title: Analogous hues: colour theory revisited
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do sunsets of red, orange and yellow look beautiful together but rarely clash?
objectives: To understand how analogous colour schemes create harmony in a composition
successCriteria: All: identify analogous colours on the colour wheel
Most: mix a smooth analogous range from three neighbouring hues
Some: use one complementary accent to make an analogous scheme stand out
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: white light splits into a spectrum of colours
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on colour in creation

keywords.def: the name of a pure colour, such as red or blue-green
three to five colours next to each other on the wheel

hook.text: Why do sunsets of red, orange and yellow look beautiful together but rarely clash?
hook.a: They are neighbours on the colour wheel: analogous colours share hues, so they harmonise.

islamicLink.text: Allah draws attention to the different colours of the earth, mountains and creatures as signs for those who reflect (Fatir 35:27-28). Studying colour in nature is a way of reflecting on His creation.

starter.q: Which feels calmer: soft blue waves or red zig-zags?
What is the complementary colour of red?
What does abstract art use instead of recognisable things?

teach.heading: The twelve-hue wheel
bullets: Tertiary: a primary mixed with a neighbour secondary
teach.note: Show the wheel; name the tertiaries.

teach.heading: Analogous schemes
teach.note: Examples: yellow, yellow-orange, orange; blue, blue-green, green.

teach.heading: Mixing a smooth range
bullets: Add the next a little at a time
Add tints with white, shades with a touch of the complementary
teach.note: Model a seven-step range from yellow to orange.

model.problem: Mix a range from yellow to red-orange.
steps: Each next box: add a little more red
model.answer: Seven even steps across neighbouring hues

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which is an analogous scheme?
check.why: Analogous colours are neighbours; red and green, and yellow and purple, are complementary opposites.

practice.q: Name the two neighbours of orange on the twelve-hue wheel.
practice.a: Red-orange and yellow-orange.
practice.model: Teacher puts a finger on orange and moves one step each way: red-orange, yellow-orange.

practice.q: Make blue lighter without changing the hue. How?
practice.a: Add white (a tint).

practice.q: Why add a small complementary accent?
practice.a: It contrasts and draws the eye, making the scheme livelier.

independent.q: Core: Paint or colour a seven-step analogous range, then a tint and shade strip for the middle hue.
independent.a: Even steps between neighbours; a tint and shade strip.
independent.model: Teacher paints steps 1 to 3 on camera.

independent.q: Extend: Colour your abstract piece from last lesson again in an analogous scheme. Compare the two versions.
independent.a: A second version with a written comparison.

independent.q: Stretch: Add one complementary accent to your analogous version and explain its effect.
independent.a: For example: a small blue shape in an orange scheme becomes the focal point.

exit.q: Analogous colours are... A) opposite on the wheel B) next to each other on the wheel C) only greys
exit.a: B) next to each other on the wheel
options: Next to each other on the wheel

exit.q: Big question: why do sunset colours rarely clash?
exit.a: They are analogous neighbours, so they share hues and harmonise.

lessons.homework: Photograph three analogous colour schemes in nature or at home (for example leaves) and upload them to the portal.
lessons.send: SEND: a printed colour wheel to colour in. EAL: hue, tint, shade glossary. Stretch: a split-complementary scheme.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 8 (abstract art; analogous hues)
At home: sketchbook or A4 paper, pencils, coloured pencils or paints, ruler, three household objects
Twelve-hue colour wheel and mixing strip (pupil PDF)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Abstract art, still life and analogous colour
lessons.title: Still life to abstract: simplifying shapes
lessons.bigQuestion: How few lines do you need before a drawing of a jug still looks like a jug?
objectives: To understand how artists simplify observed objects into abstract shapes
successCriteria: All: draw a still life object in outline from observation
Most: simplify it in three stages towards abstract
Some: rearrange and overlap the simplified shapes into a balanced composition
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: logos and icons are simplified drawings
lessons.smsc: Moral: deciding what matters most and leaving out the rest

keywords.def: remove detail to keep the essential shape
draw in a simpler, designed way
the arrangement of shapes on the page

hook.text: How few lines do you need before a drawing of a jug still looks like a jug?
hook.a: Often only a few: the outline and the handle. That is simplification.

starter.a: A small area of the opposite colour to draw the eye.
The space around and between objects.

teach.heading: From real to abstract
teach.note: Show the three stages of one jug.

teach.heading: Ways to simplify
teach.note: Show photos of designed icons (a jug icon) to compare.

teach.heading: Model: three stages
teach.note: Model with a jug.

model.problem: Turn a jug into an abstract design.
steps: Stage 2: body becomes a rectangle, handle a semicircle
Stage 3: repeat and overlap the shapes, rotate one
model.answer: A balanced design that began as a jug

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which step is simplifying?
options: Replacing a curved handle with a semicircle
check.why: Simplifying removes detail and keeps the essential shape.

practice.q: Draw a bottle in three stages: observed, simplified, abstract.
practice.a: Three thumbnails moving from realistic to abstract.
practice.model: Teacher draws stage 1 and stage 2 of the bottle, naming what was removed.

independent.q: Core: Choose two objects from your still life. Draw each in three stages, then combine the stage 3 shapes into one A5 composition.
independent.a: Two three-stage strips and a combined composition with overlap and balance.
independent.model: Teacher combines the jug and bottle stage 3 shapes, overlapping them and rotating one.

independent.q: Extend: Write in the portal response box what you removed and why. Start: 'I simplified... by...'
independent.a: For example: I simplified the mug by turning its curves into a rectangle and a semicircle.

exit.q: To simplify means... A) add detail B) keep the essential shape and remove detail C) copy exactly
exit.a: B) keep the essential shape and remove detail
options: Keep the essential shape and remove detail

exit.q: Big question: how few lines did your simplest stage need? Was it still recognisable?
exit.a: For example: five lines; yes, the handle made it recognisable.

lessons.homework: Simplify one object from the kitchen in three stages in your sketchbook.
lessons.send: SEND: a three-box strip with stage 1 given. EAL: simplify, shape, stage. Stretch: simplify towards a single continuous line.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 8 (abstract art; analogous hues)
At home: sketchbook or A4 paper, pencils, coloured pencils or paints, ruler, three household objects
Three-stage simplification strip (pupil PDF)

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Abstract art, still life and analogous colour
lessons.title: A still life series with Islamic pattern and Hundertwasser elements
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens if you fill a simple jug shape with an eight-pointed star pattern? Does it stay a jug?
objectives: To understand how combining observed objects, Islamic geometric pattern and Hundertwasser's bold colour creates a personal series
successCriteria: All: add a geometric pattern to a simplified still life
Most: use Hundertwasser-style bold outlines, spirals and bright colour in part of the design
Some: plan a series of three variations and explain the changes
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rotational symmetry and constructions with a compass
lessons.smsc: Cultural: Islamic geometric design alongside a modern European artist

keywords.def: a set of artworks that develop one idea
a shape or pattern that repeats
Austrian artist and architect known for spirals, bright colour and wavy lines
a design made from repeated regular shapes

hook.text: What happens if you fill a simple jug shape with an eight-pointed star pattern? Does it stay a jug?
hook.a: It becomes both: an object and a pattern. The shape gives structure, the pattern gives rhythm.

islamicLink.text: Islamic geometric patterns grow from simple constructions with a compass and ruler, repeating without end. Many see in them a reminder of the order and unity in Allah's creation. We use these patterns as motifs, keeping to objects, plants and geometry.

starter.a: Keep the essential shape and remove detail.

starter.q: How many points does an eight-pointed star have, and how many squares overlap to make it?
starter.a: Eight points, made from two overlapping squares.
A shape or pattern that repeats.

teach.heading: Hundertwasser
teach.note: Show a photo of the Hundertwasserhaus in Vienna (a building, no figures).

teach.heading: Islamic pattern as motif
teach.note: Show the compass construction quickly (the full Islamic art unit is caught up in Autumn 2027).

teach.heading: Combining the three
teach.note: Model one design.

model.problem: Combine a jug, a star pattern and Hundertwasser colour.
steps: Draw the simplified jug shape large
Fill the body with an eight-pointed star grid
Surround it with spirals and wavy bands
Colour: bright analogous bands with a complementary accent
model.answer: One design joining observation, pattern and bold colour

teach.heading: A series
bullets: Change one thing each time: colour, pattern or layout
teach.note: Thumbnails first.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which feature is typical of Hundertwasser?
check.why: He used spirals, wavy lines and bright colour and rejected straight lines.

practice.q: Draw three thumbnails of the same jug, each with a different pattern or colour plan.
practice.a: Three different variations planned.
practice.model: Teacher draws thumbnail 1 (star pattern inside) and thumbnail 2 (spirals outside), saying what changes.

independent.q: Core: Make the first full piece of your series on A4: simplified objects, a geometric motif and Hundertwasser-style colour and spirals.
independent.a: An A4 piece combining all three elements.
independent.model: Teacher draws the jug and starts the star grid.

independent.q: Extend: Write in the portal response box how your next two pieces will change. Start: 'In piece two I will change...'
independent.a: For example: In piece two I will change the colours to a cool analogous scheme.

exit.q: A series is... A) one artwork B) a set of artworks developing one idea C) a type of paint
exit.a: B) a set of artworks developing one idea
options: A set of artworks developing one idea

exit.q: Big question: when you fill a jug with a star pattern, is it still a jug? Explain.
exit.a: Both: the shape stays a jug, the pattern turns it into a design.

lessons.homework: Finish piece one and sketch piece two of your series (developing the composition continues as independent study).
lessons.send: SEND: a printed star grid to trace into the shape. EAL: spiral, pattern, series. Stretch: add a calligraphy word (such as 'shukr' شُكْر, gratitude) as a motif.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 8 (abstract art; analogous hues)
At home: sketchbook or A4 paper, pencils, coloured pencils or paints, ruler, three household objects
Compass and ruler
Eight-pointed star grid template (pupil PDF)

pictures.alt: An eight-pointed star in zellige tiles

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Abstract art, still life and analogous colour
lessons.title: Finish and evaluate the abstract composition
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you know when an artwork is finished?
objectives: To understand how to refine and evaluate an abstract composition against clear criteria
successCriteria: All: finish one piece with neat edges and even colour
Most: evaluate it with two strengths and one target linked to the criteria
Some: compare it with an artist's work using art vocabulary
lessons.crossCurricular: English: writing an evaluation with evidence
lessons.smsc: Social: giving and receiving feedback with good manners (adab)

keywords.def: judge strengths and areas to improve
how the visual weight is spread

hook.text: How do you know when an artwork is finished?
hook.a: When every part supports the idea and changing anything would weaken it: you check against criteria.

starter.q: Which artist used spirals and bright colour?
Name one way to simplify a shape.
starter.a: For example: replace curves with straight lines.

teach.heading: Refining
teach.note: Show a before and after detail.

teach.heading: Evaluation criteria
bullets: Balance and a clear focal point
teach.note: These are the assessment criteria (portal rubric).

teach.heading: Model evaluation
teach.note: Model.

steps: WWW: the analogous oranges harmonise and the blue star is a clear focal point
WWW: the jug is simplified but still recognisable
EBI: the left side is busy; balance it with a calm area
Link: like Hundertwasser, the spirals add movement
model.answer: Two strengths, one target, one artist link

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which is the most useful EBI?
options: Balance the busy left side with a calm area of one colour
check.why: A useful target is specific and says how to improve.

practice.q: Write one WWW for the slide example using the word 'harmonise' or 'focal point'.
practice.a: For example: The analogous colours harmonise and the blue star creates a focal point.
practice.model: Teacher writes the WWW from the model, underlining the art word.

independent.q: Core: Refine your best piece from the series (edges, colour, focal point), then photograph and upload it.
independent.model: Teacher refines one corner on camera.

independent.q: Extend: Write your evaluation in the portal response box: two WWW, one EBI, one artist link. Start: 'What went well...'
independent.a: A specific evaluation using art vocabulary and the criteria.

independent.q: Stretch: Give one classmate kind, specific feedback in the portal.
independent.a: One strength and one specific target.

exit.q: A useful target is... A) vague B) specific and says how to improve C) about someone else
exit.a: B) specific and says how to improve
options: Specific and says how to improve

exit.q: Big question: how did you decide your piece was finished?
exit.a: It met the criteria and changing more would weaken it.

lessons.homework: Read your teacher's feedback in the portal and write one sentence on what you will do next time.
lessons.send: SEND: evaluation frame with sentence starters. EAL: WWW and EBI phrases. Stretch: compare with Kandinsky in 100 words.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 8 (abstract art; analogous hues)
At home: sketchbook or A4 paper, pencils, coloured pencils or paints, ruler, three household objects
Abstract composition assessment rubric and evaluation frame (portal)

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The hand: drawing to clay sculpture
lessons.title: Anatomy of the hand: bones and proportion
lessons.bigQuestion: Allah says He is able 'to proportion his fingertips' (Al-Qiyamah 75:4). What is amazing about how a hand is made?
objectives: To understand the structure and proportions of the hand so drawings look believable
successCriteria: All: name the three groups of hand bones
Most: use proportion rules to plan a hand drawing
Some: explain how structure helps drawing
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the design of the human hand

hook.text: Allah says He is able 'to proportion his fingertips' (Al-Qiyamah 75:4). What is amazing about how a hand is made?
hook.a: 27 bones, joints that bend just right, unique fingerprints: precise design.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Yes. [We are] Able [even] to proportion his fingertips.' (Al-Qiyamah 75:4).

starter.q: A vanishing point is used in ...

starter.a: Line, shape, form, colour, tone, texture, space.

teach.heading: Bones of the hand
teach.note: Diagram of hand bones (skeletal diagram, not a person).

teach.heading: Proportion rules
bullets: Palm about as long as the middle finger
Knuckles form a curve, not a line
teach.note: House rule: the hand study only (no face or figure), kept from the Year 8 intent (TO CONFIRM with the owner). If the owner decides against it, use the same techniques on a natural form (pine cone, shell or seed head).

teach.heading: Simplify to shapes
cycle: Thumb from the side of the palm

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: How many bones are in the human hand?

practice.q: Draw a simplified hand: a box palm and cylinder fingers in three sections.
practice.a: A structural hand drawing.
practice.model: I do: box for the palm, three cylinders per finger, two for the thumb.

independent.q: Sketchbook: three structural studies of your own hand (open, side, closed) using shapes and proportion lines.
independent.model: The teacher draws the open hand study on camera.

independent.q: Extend: label the bone groups on one study.
Stretch: measure your palm and middle finger and compare.

exit.q: Phalanges are ...
exit.a: finger bones

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Allah says He is able 'to proportion his fingertips' (Al-Qiyamah 75:4). What is amazing about how a hand is made?
exit.a: 27 bones, joints that bend just right, unique fingerprints: precise design.

lessons.homework: Draw your hand holding a household object (a cup or pen).
lessons.send: SEND: chunked tasks, a key word glossary and sentence starters in the pupil PDF. EAL: key terms with definitions and examples. Stretch: evaluate, weigh up both sides and reach a justified judgement.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The hand: drawing to clay sculpture
lessons.title: Observational drawing of the hand: line and tone
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is drawing what you see harder than drawing what you know?
objectives: To understand how to draw a hand from observation using contour line and tone
successCriteria: All: draw the contour of my hand from observation
Most: add tone with a clear light source
Some: vary line weight to show depth
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: careful looking as gratitude

keywords.def: the outline and edges of a form
how thick or dark a line is

hook.text: Why is drawing what you see harder than drawing what you know?
hook.a: Our brain simplifies; observation means looking at real shapes and shadows, not symbols.

starter.q: What shape is the palm simplified to?

teach.heading: Blind contour warm-up
bullets: Look at your hand, not the page
teach.note: House rule: the hand study only (no face or figure), kept from the Year 8 intent (TO CONFIRM with the owner). If the owner decides against it, use the same techniques on a natural form (pine cone, shell or seed head).

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: With the lamp on the left, the darkest shadows are ...
options: on the right side of the fingers
check.why: Shadows fall away from the light.

practice.q: Do a 2-minute blind contour of your hand.
practice.a: A continuous line drawing.
practice.model: I do: eyes on my hand, pencil moving slowly with my eye.

independent.q: Observational drawing: your hand holding an object, with contour and three tones from one light source.
independent.model: The teacher draws and tones a section on camera.

independent.q: Extend: add cross-hatching in the darkest areas.
Stretch: vary line weight to push the near fingers forward.

exit.q: Highlights are ...
exit.a: the lightest areas

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Why is drawing what you see harder than drawing what you know?
exit.a: Our brain simplifies; observation means looking at real shapes and shadows, not symbols.

lessons.homework: Two more 5-minute hand studies in different positions.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The hand: drawing to clay sculpture
lessons.title: Hand gestures: a series of drawings
lessons.bigQuestion: Hands can show du'a, welcome, help and work. Which gestures carry meaning without words?
objectives: To understand how a series of drawings can show movement and meaning
successCriteria: All: draw three different hand gestures
Most: keep proportions consistent across the series

hook.text: What makes a finished piece look professional rather than rushed?
hook.a: Clean edges, even colour, a clear focal point and care in every detail.
